Why coordinated FDI is harder to detect

Simple FDI lowers only reported active power P. Because the report still carries the original V, I and PF, the rule P = V × I × PF no longer holds and Layer 1 flags it immediately.

Coordinated stealth FDI lowers the reported current and then recomputes P from the reported V, I and PF. Every report is internally consistent, so Layer 1 passes. Example: actual 230 V × 10 A × 0.95 = 2185 W; reported 230 V × 5 A × 0.95 = 1092.5 W.

The physical load is unchanged, so the independently measured feeder power still includes it. Layer 2 compares that feeder measurement with the sum of reported consumer powers. When the gap exceeds the threshold for the configured number of consecutive ticks, a critical alert is raised. This shows that reported data cannot be trusted, not which meter or attack caused it; narrowing it down needs cross-meter analysis, sub-feeder measurements and field inspection.

This tool is a deterministic rule-based simulation with synthetic noise. It uses no machine learning and does not claim to identify attackers.
